solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: A row of homes

definitions.note: the article goes with the noun: a domestic is a row
an adjectival phrase, matching the adjective sense

blocks.note: first meaning: British slang for a household quarrel, the kind neighbours call the police about
second meaning: the adjective for things belonging to the household

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one phrase, a terrace of houses, but splits after 'row': a row that rhymes with 'cow' is a quarrel, and 'of homes' is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun the word is British slang for a family quarrel; as an adjective it describes anything relating to the household.

clue.text: Might one really like an old Aussie soldier?

definitions.note: a person who digs, i.e. really likes, something

blocks.note: first meaning: to dig is slang for to like a lot, so one who does so
second meaning: the nickname for Australian and New Zealand troops of the First World War

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a person could be fond of an elderly Australian veteran.
explanation.walkthrough: The question frame asks whether 'one who digs' could also be the old soldier; it can, as both senses share one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang verb 'dig' means enjoy, giving an agent noun; separately, Australian infantry of the Great War were nicknamed after trench work.

clue.text: Bit of music expected with boat race coverage

indicators.note: a bit is only a small piece, so just the opening letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of music
what is asked of you is what is expected of you

explanation.surface: A snippet of music is anticipated during the television coverage of the Oxford and Cambridge rowing race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boat race' is not rowing: it is Cockney rhyming slang for face, so 'boat race coverage' means having the face covered.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone wearing a mask has a covering over the face, which rhyming slang calls the boat race.

clue.text: Constant or variable dates before Lent?

indicators.note: something variable changes its form, so these letters take a different order

blocks.note: the five letters rearranged
Lent is the Christian season of fasting

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the dates leading up to Lent are fixed or movable, since Easter moves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' places one piece ahead of the other in this down answer. 'Constant' and 'variable' look like a mathematical pair, but only 'Constant' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A steadfast person is constant: firm, loyal and unwavering, the adjectival synonym.

clue.text: So in pain, laid up in a foreign capital

indicators.note: things that are up are in disarray or out of order, as in 'what's up', so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: all twelve letters used

explanation.surface: A traveller, suffering badly, is laid up in bed in some capital city abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laid up' reads as bedridden, but 'laid' is part of the fodder and 'up' alone signals the jumble. The capital is of a US state, not a country.
explanation.definitionFit: Indianapolis is the state capital of Indiana, which for a British setter is a capital city abroad.

clue.text: One completely lacking in IT experience

definitions.text: One completely lacking in IT experience

blocks.clueFragment: One completely lacking in IT experience
blocks.note: surface reading: someone who has never used computers
setter's reading: 'it' is a coy euphemism for sex, so someone with no sexual experience at all

explanation.walkthrough: IT in capitals looks like information technology; read as the pronoun 'it', it is the old euphemism for sex.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has never had sexual intercourse is called by this word, which also loosely means a novice.

clue.text: Criminal, larcenous to an extent, or altogether

indicators.note: only to an extent means partly, so just part of the run of letters is wanted

blocks.note: found across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A crook is called somewhat thieving, or perhaps thoroughly so.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters bridge the comma, ending one word and starting the next.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means in total, as in 'twenty people came in all', a straightforward synonym for altogether.

clue.text: Moral excellence can be found in GOSH

blocks.note: first meaning: the quality of being virtuous
second meaning: a mild exclamation of surprise

explanation.surface: Virtue is to be found at Great Ormond Street Hospital, the London children's hospital known as GOSH.
explanation.walkthrough: GOSH in capitals suggests the acronym for Great Ormond Street Hospital; it is simply the exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names virtue as a noun and also serves as a mild oath of surprise, interchangeable with 'gosh'.

clue.text: No reason to consume starter of niffy rhubarb

indicators.note: what consumes something takes it inside, so one piece goes within the other
a starter is the first course, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: having no sense is having no reason
the first letter of niffy, British slang for smelly

explanation.surface: There is no cause to eat the opening portion of some smelly rhubarb.
explanation.walkthrough: Rhubarb is the defining word, not the food: in Britain it also means foolish talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhubarb is British slang for nonsense, from actors murmuring the word to mimic background chatter.

clue.text: See just one man regularly take it easy

blocks.note: first meaning: to date one partner exclusively
second meaning: to proceed carefully, without rushing

explanation.surface: Advice to someone: commit to one boyfriend and relax a little.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' tempts a solver to take alternate letters, but here it is part of the plain dating sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means to be in a settled exclusive relationship, and as a command it means be careful and calm.

clue.text: Primate and bishop getting a blessing

blocks.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
taken as written
a boon is a blessing or benefit

explanation.surface: An archbishop and a bishop together receive a benediction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primate' with 'bishop' points to an archbishop; it is the animal sense, an ape or monkey.
explanation.definitionFit: The baboon is a large African monkey, and monkeys belong to the order of mammals called primates.

clue.text: US anthem played with care around Hue mostly

indicators.note: a piece played can be performed in new ways, so these letters are rearranged
mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
to go around something is to enclose it, so one piece surrounds the other

blocks.note: taken as written, as fodder
taken as written, as fodder
the word without its last letter

explanation.surface: America's national anthem is performed carefully around the Vietnamese city of Hue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'US' looks like the United States attached to 'anthem'; it is the pronoun us, the definition, and the anagram covers only the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: We, all people collectively, make up humankind, so the pronoun 'us' stands for humanity as a whole.

clue.text: Polish and English blokes heading for Deal

indicators.note: a heading sits at the top, so only the opening letter of the word is used

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
blokes is British slang for men
the first letter of Deal

explanation.surface: Polish and English men make their way to Deal, a seaside town in Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' at the start of the clue is capitalised to look like the nationality; it is the verb, to refine.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend a text is to correct and improve it, just as polishing writing refines it.

clue.text: An extremely fair woman in Barnet

definitions.text: An extremely fair woman in Barnet

blocks.clueFragment: An extremely fair woman in Barnet
blocks.note: surface reading: a very beautiful woman living in Barnet, a north London borough
setter's reading: barnet is rhyming slang for hair (Barnet Fair), so a woman whose hair is very pale

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair' suggests beauty and Barnet a place; in rhyming slang a barnet is your hair, and fair hair of the palest greyish shade has a name.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the palest, greyish shade of blonde hair, so a woman with it is extremely fair-haired.

clue.text: Ridiculous past haircuts and jumpers

indicators.note: something ridiculous is absurd and disordered, so these letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: all twelve letters used

explanation.surface: Someone mocks the absurd hairstyles and knitted sweaters of earlier decades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumpers' sits beside haircuts as fashion, since in Britain a jumper is a sweater; here it means people who jump.
explanation.definitionFit: Parachutists leap from aircraft, so they are jumpers in the literal sense of people who jump.

clue.text: Damn American version of “Limeys”?

definitions.note: an American exclamation used in place of 'damn'

blocks.note: first meaning: a folksy American oath, a softened 'damnation'
second meaning, read in two parts: Limeys were British sailors

explanation.surface: An American's damning way of referring to the British.
explanation.walkthrough: Limey, American slang for a Briton, began as a name for Royal Navy sailors, who drank lime juice against scurvy; a tar is a sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarnation is a mild American euphemism for damnation, used as an exclamation where 'damn' would be ruder.

clue.text: Players’ union to ring City about level playing field?

indicators.note: turning about means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards
a ring encircles, so one piece is placed around the other

blocks.note: Equity is the British trade union for actors, who are players
LA is Los Angeles, a common crossword city

explanation.surface: A sports union phones the club about making a pitch fair to both sides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Players' and 'City' suggest football; the players are actors and the City is Los Angeles.
explanation.definitionFit: A level playing field is a figurative state where all have the same chances, which is fairness of treatment.

clue.text: Turn quickly by bar as Cherry is naked

blocks.note: to leaf through a book is to turn its pages quickly
bar and less both mean except, without

explanation.surface: Someone spins round at the pub counter because a woman called Cherry has no clothes on.
explanation.walkthrough: Cherry is capitalised to look like a name, but it is the tree, which stands naked of foliage in winter.
explanation.definitionFit: A bare tree in winter has lost its foliage, so naked here describes branches without any covering.

clue.text: Square knot I’m to unravel?

indicators.note: unravelling undoes a tangle and lays its strands out differently, so these letters are reordered

blocks.note: all twelve letters used

explanation.surface: A sailor faces the job of untying a reef knot.
explanation.walkthrough: A square knot is a reef knot, but here the words are fodder; read whole, the clue describes the puzzle a solver must work out, and it ends in the symbol itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A question mark stands for something puzzling still to be resolved, the knotty problem the clue describes.

clue.text: For each exercise, study closely with care

blocks.note: per means for each, as in miles per hour
to exercise a right is to use it

explanation.surface: For every workout, examine your technique carefully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exercise' suggests PE or training, but it is the verb meaning to employ.
explanation.definitionFit: To peruse is to read or examine something thoroughly, though in loose use it has come to mean skim.

clue.text: Run if snake is found under loo’s lid

indicators.note: a lid is the top of something, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: the first letter of loo, British slang for toilet
the adder is Britain's venomous snake

explanation.surface: Advice to flee should you find a snake lurking beneath the toilet seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run' looks like an order to flee; it is a run in tights, which the British call a ladder. 'Under' puts the snake below in this down answer, a nod to snakes and ladders.
explanation.definitionFit: A ladder is the British word for a run, a vertical line of unravelled stitches in stockings or tights.

clue.text: Show no thanks or fondness of feeling

indicators.note: 'no' means without, so these letters are taken away

blocks.note: affectation is a show, a pretence put on for effect
ta is British informal for thanks

explanation.surface: Someone shows neither gratitude nor warmth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show no thanks' reads as ingratitude; 'Show' is a noun, and the British 'ta' comes out of its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Affection is warmth and tenderness felt towards someone, matching fondness of feeling as a direct synonym.

clue.text: Bed with short brown cloth cover?

indicators.note: cutting something short removes its end, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: a cot is a small bed
tan, a light brown, without its final letter

explanation.surface: A bed comes with a short brown fabric bedspread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The cloth' means the clergy, so a cloth cover is a garment worn by clergy or choristers.
explanation.definitionFit: A cotta is a short white surplice worn over a cassock, a covering garment for those of the cloth.

clue.text: Part of old theatre article Times rejected

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: an is the indefinite article
an era is a period, one of the times

explanation.surface: A section of a historic playhouse, featured in a piece the Times newspaper turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: Times is capitalised to suggest the newspaper; it just means periods.
explanation.definitionFit: The arena was the central sanded floor of a Roman amphitheatre, where the gladiatorial shows were staged.

clue.text: Some deride a teacher … imagine

indicators.note: some means a portion only, so the letters sit inside the words that follow

blocks.note: runs across all three words

explanation.surface: People mock a teacher, just picture it.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis separates the wordplay from the one-word definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To ideate is to form ideas or conceive something in the mind, so it serves as a formal synonym.

clue.text: Worn out army uniform needs alteration ultimately

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: fatigues are soldiers' work clothes
the final letter of alteration

explanation.surface: A threadbare military uniform has to be altered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worn out' seems to describe the uniform as threadbare; it is the definition, meaning exhausted.
explanation.definitionFit: Fatigued means exhausted or very tired, the usual sense of worn out when applied to a person.

clue.text: I agree, the old chap smothers son

definitions.note: a phrase standing for the person who always says it

indicators.note: to smother is to cover completely, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: ye is the archaic form of the
S is the abbreviation for son
a chap is a man

explanation.surface: Someone concedes that an elderly father suffocates his own boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The old chap' reads as a father, but splits into the archaic article and a man, which together enclose the son.
explanation.definitionFit: A yes-man is a sycophant who always agrees with superiors, so the words 'I agree' epitomise him.

clue.text: One ruminates about India always being poetic

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
IND is a standard abbreviation for India
e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, meaning always

explanation.surface: A thinker reflects on India's timeless poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruminates' suggests deep thinking, but it is the literal sense of chewing the cud. 'Poetic' tells you to use the verse spelling of ever.
explanation.definitionFit: Reindeer are ruminants, cud-chewing animals with multi-chambered stomachs, like cattle and deer.
